title: The Great Compassion Mantra (Dabeizhou)
summary: Before dawn in the temple hall the wooden fish begins to knock, and eighty-four lines of Sanskrit flow out one after another -- this is the Great Compassion Mantra (Dabeizhou), born of the vow-power of the Thousand-Handed, Thousand-Eyed Avalokitesvara. It is the long dharani Taiwanese Buddhists recite most in their morning and evening services, and many lean on it to steady the mind, dissolve misfortune, and pray for blessings.
content:
Walk into the morning or evening service of almost any Buddhist temple in Taiwan and you will hear it -- the Great Compassion Mantra, formally titled "The Great Compassion Heart Dharani of the Thousand-Handed and Thousand-Eyed Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva," eighty-four lines in all. It is an indispensable part of temple liturgy and one of the long mantras that lay practitioners keep most readily on their lips.

【Origin of the Mantra】
The Great Compassion Heart Dharani Sutra tells it this way: countless eons ago, Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva heard this mantra for the first time before the Thousand Radiance Stillness Tathagata. After hearing it just once, the bodhisattva leapt from the first bhumi (stage of a bodhisattva) straight to the eighth, and in great joy made this vow: "If in the future I am able to benefit and bring peace to all sentient beings, may I instantly manifest a thousand hands and a thousand eyes." No sooner were the words spoken than a thousand hands and a thousand eyes appeared upon the bodhisattva's body. Avalokitesvara later told the assembly: "If any sentient being recites and upholds this Great Compassion Dharani, they shall not suffer fifteen kinds of evil death and shall obtain fifteen kinds of good rebirth."

【Content of the Mantra】
The mantra is mostly a phonetic transliteration from Sanskrit. It opens with "Namo heladana duolayeye" (taking refuge in the Three Jewels), continues with "Namo aliye" (taking refuge in the Holy One), and only then enters the core of the mantra. Each line is regarded as a manifestation of Avalokitesvara's vow power, answering to a different work of compassionate rescue. Most people cannot actually read the Sanskrit, but in the Buddhist understanding the mantra's power comes from the vibration of the sound itself together with the sincerity of the one reciting -- you need not grasp every word to receive its blessing.

【Methods of Practice】
A daily commitment is usually seven, twenty-one, or one hundred and eight recitations. Before you begin, wash your hands and rinse your mouth, sit upright with palms joined, recite "Namo Great Compassion Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva" three times, and only then start the mantra; a string of mala beads at hand helps keep count. Keep the pace even, neither rushed nor dragging, and enunciate clearly. Those who have walked this road usually suggest beginners recite along with a recording first, then chant alone once it feels familiar. For many Taiwanese Buddhists, being able to recite the whole Great Compassion Mantra from memory is an unforgettable milestone on the path.

【Great Compassion Water】
Clean water blessed with the Great Compassion Mantra is called "Great Compassion Water," and it is much valued in Taiwanese folk religion. The method is simple: take a cup of clean water, recite the Great Compassion Mantra seven times (or more) before a Buddha image, and after each round trace the sacred syllable "Om" on the water's surface with a finger; when you finish, it has become Great Compassion Water. Devotees believe drinking it can dissolve karmic obstacles, ease illness, and purify body and mind. Major Buddhist organizations in Taiwan, such as Dharma Drum Mountain and Fo Guang Shan, often keep Great Compassion Water on hand for devotees during dharma assemblies.

【Merits and Blessings】
The sutras record no shortage of merits for upholding the mantra: at the moment of death being received by the hands of the Buddhas of the ten directions, never falling into the three evil realms, having one's wishes fulfilled, and the wiping away of all karmic obstacles. Taiwanese folk culture also passes down all kinds of miracle stories -- someone gravely ill who recovered after sustained recitation, someone who came through disaster unscathed. Such accounts are hard to verify one by one, but the peace of mind and inner strength the Great Compassion Mantra gives those who recite it are real enough.

【Practice in Taiwan】
Nearly every major practice center in Taiwan works the Great Compassion Mantra into its daily liturgy; in the group services of Dharma Drum Mountain, Tzu Chi Foundation, and Fo Guang Shan it is among the most common practices. On the 19th day of the second, sixth, and ninth lunar months -- Guanyin's birthday, enlightenment day, and renunciation day respectively -- temples hold "Great Compassion Repentance Assemblies" built around the mantra, coming together to repent and to pray.

title: The Heart Sutra (Bore Boluomiduo Xingjing)
summary: Two hundred and sixty characters. The people who have copied it, chanted it, and worn it engraved on a gold pendant span the whole island -- this is the Heart Sutra, the shortest of Buddhist scriptures yet the one that has sunk deepest into the culture. Almost everyone has heard its line, "form is emptiness."
content:
The Prajna Paramita Heart Sutra is known simply as the Heart Sutra. Xuanzang's translation runs to just 260 characters, yet it is the most widely circulated Buddhist scripture of all, regarded as the whole 600-volume Great Prajna Sutra boiled down to its essence. In Taiwan it is not only a Buddhist's daily recitation but has long since seeped into everyday Chinese culture.

【Core Philosophy】
The whole sutra turns on a single word: "emptiness" (sunyata). It opens: "When Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva was practicing the deep Prajna Paramita, he illuminated the five aggregates and saw that they are all empty, thus transcending all suffering and distress." With the wisdom of deep prajna the bodhisattva sees that the five aggregates that make up all existence -- form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness -- are all, at root, empty. Then comes the most famous line of all: "Form is not different from emptiness, emptiness is not different from form; form is emptiness, emptiness is form" -- the material world and emptiness are not two opposed things but one reality seen from two sides. This is not nihilism; it means that everything arises through the coming-together of causes and conditions, with no permanent, unchanging self-nature. See through this, and attachment loosens, arriving at the state of "a mind with no hindrances, and because there are no hindrances, there is no fear, and one is far removed from inverted thinking and fantasy, ultimately attaining nirvana."

【The Closing Mantra】
The Heart Sutra concludes with the mantra "Gate gate paragate parasamgate bodhi svaha" (in Sanskrit), meaning "Gone, gone, gone beyond, gone completely beyond, awakening, so be it!" This is the summation mantra of the entire Heart Sutra, gathering the full force of prajna wisdom into these few words.

【Sutra-Copying Culture】
In Taiwan, copying the Heart Sutra by hand could not be a more common form of practice. It is more than penmanship -- writing it out one character at a time takes concentration and calm, and every stroke is a kind of quiet conversation with the text. Many temples (Dharma Drum Mountain among them) have set up "sutra-copying rooms" where people can copy in stillness. Some vow to copy it a thousand or even ten thousand times, dedicating the accumulated merit to someone on their mind. Even Taiwan's creative arts market now turns out all kinds of beautifully designed Heart Sutra copybooks, linking old practice to modern taste.

【Everyday Applications】
The Heart Sutra is almost everywhere in Taiwan:
- The required recitation of temple morning and evening services.
- Chanted for the deceased during funerary ceremonies.
- A recurring subject for calligraphers.
- Engraved by jewelers onto gold amulets and bracelets.
- Printed in full on protective amulets.
- Silently recited by many people to calm anxiety and steady a restless mind.

【Methods of Recitation】
The Heart Sutra is short, which makes it perfect for daily recitation. Recite it three to seven times just after waking in the morning or before bed at night. Keep an even pace, enunciate clearly, and let it ride the rhythm of your breath. Some suggest getting a rough sense of the meaning before you recite, but even if it stays beyond you, reciting sincerely still lets the mind settle bit by bit.

title: The Six-Syllable Mantra (Om Mani Padme Hum)
summary: Recite it while you walk, while you wait for the bus, before you fall asleep -- six syllables, "Om Mani Padme Hum," the root heart mantra of Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva and the most widely recited Buddhist mantra in the world. Anytime, anywhere, you can open your mouth and begin.
content:
Six syllables, "Om Mani Padme Hum," form the root heart mantra of Avalokitesvara (Guanyin) Bodhisattva -- one of the most widely spread, most often recited Buddhist mantras anywhere in the world. In Taiwan, practitioners of both the Chinese and the Tibetan Buddhist traditions keep it on their lips.

【Meaning of the Six Syllables】
Each syllable stands for one of Avalokitesvara's compassionate vows and works of liberation:
- Om: the three mysteries of the Buddha's body, speech, and mind; the primordial sound that begins every mantra, the fundamental vibration of the universe.
- Ma: the perfection of patience (kshanti paramita), dispelling jealousy and closing the gate to the realm of the asuras (demi-gods).
- Ni: the perfection of moral discipline (sila paramita), dispelling desire and easing the sufferings of the human realm.
- Pa: the perfection of diligence (virya paramita), dispelling ignorance and closing the gate to the animal realm.
- Dme (Me): the perfection of meditation (dhyana paramita), dispelling miserliness and closing the gate to the realm of hungry ghosts.
- Hum: the perfection of wisdom (prajna paramita), dispelling hatred and closing the gate to the hell realm.
Taken together, the six syllables picture Avalokitesvara using the wisdom and compassion of the six paramitas to rescue beings across all six realms from the cycle of rebirth.

【Methods of Recitation】
This is about the easiest mantra to take up -- no special place, time, or ritual required:
- It may be recited aloud (spoken or whispered) or silently (vajra recitation, lips barely moving with no audible sound).
- It may be counted on mala beads (108 to a round) or recited without counting.
- Walking, commuting, standing in line, drifting toward sleep -- any moment will do.
- A daily commitment of at least 108 is a good aim; dedicated practitioners recite a thousand or more.
- In Taiwan the most common pronunciation is "Om Ma Ni Ba Mi Hong"; the Tibetan reading differs a little (Om Mani Peme Hung).

【Prayer Wheels】
In the Tibetan tradition the six syllables are inscribed inside prayer wheels, and one turn of the wheel counts as a single recitation. Tibetan Buddhist centers in Taiwan usually keep prayer wheels for visitors to use, and in recent years small hand-held wheels have caught on, making the practice easier still. The Six-Syllable Mantra is also inscribed on prayer flags (lung ta, or wind-horse flags); as they flutter in the wind, they are believed to scatter its blessings in every direction.

【Spread in Taiwan】
In Taiwan this mantra crosses the line between the Chinese and Tibetan traditions -- nearly every Buddhist can recite it. You hear "Om Mani Padme Hum" at temple group practice, in daily personal devotions, and at the bedside chanting for the dying. Even Taiwanese who are not especially devout will recite it a few times when they feel unsettled, taking it as a kind of comfort and protection.

title: The Green Tara Mantra
summary: "Om Tare Tuttare Ture Svaha" -- Tibetan Buddhism holds that the moment you recite this line with sincerity, Green Tara, famed for her "swift rescue," appears before you. She is the most beloved female bodhisattva of all, come precisely to clear away fear and remove obstacles.
content:
"Om Tare Tuttare Ture Svaha" -- this Green Tara Mantra is among the most popular in all of Tibetan Buddhism. Green Tara is seen as the embodiment of the tears of compassion that Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva shed, the foremost of all the Buddha Mothers, and she is known for her "swift rescue": it is said that the moment devotees recite her mantra in earnest, Green Tara comes at once to offer protection.

【The Origin of Green Tara】
Legend has it that Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva, gazing down on the suffering of all beings from Mount Potalaka, wept tears of pity that would not stop falling. The tear from the left eye became Green Tara; the tear from the right became White Tara. Green Tara stands for compassion in action -- she sits in a half-lotus posture, yet her right foot reaches forward, ever ready to rise and rescue, a sign that she does not wait passively but answers every cry for help actively and fast. Her body is emerald green, alive with vitality and active energy; her right hand forms the boon-granting mudra (palm turned outward), her left holds a blue lotus, and her whole form radiates the light of compassion.

【Analysis of the Mantra】
- Om: the universal primordial sound, standing for the three mysteries of the Buddha (body, speech, and mind).
- Tare: means "the liberator," Tara rescuing beings from the ocean of cyclic existence.
- Tuttare: means "dispelling all fears," Tara removing the eight great terrors -- lion peril (pride), elephant peril (ignorance), fire peril (anger), serpent peril (jealousy), bandit peril (wrong views), shackle peril (desire), flood peril (attachment), and demon peril (doubt).
- Ture: means "granting all accomplishments," Tara bestowing every attainment, worldly and transcendent.
- Svaha: means "perfect accomplishment," the mantra's concluding syllable, the prayer fulfilled in full.

【Merits of Recitation】
People often speak of the merits this way: fear and anxiety dissolved, disaster and accident kept at bay, safe travels, growing wisdom and merit, obstacles to practice swept aside, and the blessing and guardianship of Tara herself. In the Tibetan tradition she is held to be especially protective of women -- recited during pregnancy she is said to keep mother and child safe, and recited in the hard passages of a marriage, to bring the wisdom to make the right decisions.

【Methods of Practice】
- Simple practice: 108 recitations a day (one round of the mala), or in multiples of seven (7, 21, and so on).
- Complete practice: begin with taking refuge and generating bodhicitta, visualize Green Tara above the crown of your head radiating light to bless you, then recite the mantra, and conclude by dedicating the merit.
- Special occasions: when fear or anxiety rises, before setting out on a journey, at a hard crossroads of decision, or when praying for others.

【Spread in Taiwan】
Once Tibetan Buddhism took root in Taiwan, devotion to Green Tara flourished along with it. Tibetan Buddhist centers around the island (such as Drikung Kagyu, Karma Kagyu, and Gelug centers) hold Green Tara dharma assemblies and empowerments regularly, and many Chinese Buddhist practitioners have taken up her mantra too, folding it into daily practice. Green Tara's gentle, compassionate image, together with the "swift rescue" that marks her devotion, has made her especially dear to women practitioners in Taiwan.

title: The Cundi Dharani (Zhunti Zhou)
summary: Mother of seventy million Buddhas -- Cundi Buddha Mother, eighteen arms each holding a ritual implement, a third eye open on her brow. Her mantra, known as the "Wish-Fulfilling Mantra," may be recited by anyone, monastic or lay, pure or impure, and in Taiwan it is famous for answering every prayer.
content:
The Cundi Dharani comes from the Cundi Dharani Sutra and is the core mantra of Cundi Buddha Mother (Cundi). She is honored as the "Mother of Seven Koti (70 Million) Buddhas," a station of the highest rank. In Chinese Buddhism the Cundi Dharani is counted among the "Ten Short Mantras" and is an important part of the daily liturgy; in Taiwan a good number of practice centers take the Cundi method as their main cultivation, and its followers are many.

【Full Text of the Mantra】
"Namah saptanam samyaksambuddha kotinam. Tadyatha: Om Cale Cule Cundi Svaha."
Meaning: "Homage to the seven million perfectly enlightened Buddhas. Thus: Om, Action, Purification, Cundi, Accomplishment!"

【About Cundi Buddha Mother】
Cundi Buddha Mother usually appears with eighteen arms, each hand grasping a different ritual implement (sword, mala beads, lotus, precious vase, vajra, and so on), a sign of the infinite skillful means by which she saves sentient beings. Her face is compassionate and dignified, and three eyes gaze wide open (one on her forehead), able to see clear across past, present, and future. What sets Cundi apart is her openness: she draws no line between monastic and lay, nor between states of ritual purity and impurity. Even a lay practitioner, and even someone in a state counted ritually impure (during menstruation, for instance), may recite the Cundi Dharani. Among Buddhist mantras that kind of accessibility is extremely rare.

【Key Points of Practice】
Cundi practice turns on reciting the mantra, though the complete method has several parts:
- Dharmadhatu Purification Mantra: "Om Lam" -- recited a few times to purify the space of practice.
- Body Protection Mantra: "Om Chiling" -- recited a few times, like drawing on vajra armor to guard yourself.
- Six-Syllable Mantra: "Om Mani Padme Hum" -- recited a few times to rouse the mind of compassion.
- Main Cundi Dharani: recite "Namah saptanam..." a set number of times, with 108, 500, or 1,000 being common daily counts.
- Dedication: dedicate the merit of the practice to all sentient beings of the dharma realm.
For a simplified daily practice, just reciting the core mantra is enough, without any fixed form.

【Benefits and Merits】
The sutras record the benefits of the mantra in roughly these kinds:
- Sin elimination: erasing the ten evil deeds, the five heinous crimes, and all grave transgressions.
- Blessing increase: blessings and wisdom growing day by day.
- Wish fulfillment: every kind of worldly wish satisfied.
- Rebirth: at the moment of death, seeing Amitabha Buddha and the assembly of sages.
- Specific benefits: seeking children, recovering from illness, winning a legal dispute, passing examinations, and other worldly aspirations.
This is why the Cundi Dharani is called the "Wish-Fulfilling Mantra," renowned in Taiwanese folk religion for being effective for all prayers.

【Transmission in Taiwan】
The deepest mark on Taiwan's Cundi lineage was left by the lay scholar Nan Huai-jin. In his writings he strongly recommended the Cundi Dharani, calling it "the most suitable mantra for practice in the Dharma-Ending Age," and drew a great many Taiwanese Buddhists into the Cundi method. Today several practice centers and group cultivation communities across the island take the Cundi method as their main practice, regularly holding Cundi dharma assemblies, Cundi fire offerings (a tantric ritual that uses fire to purify karmic obstacles), and intensive group retreats.

title: The Medicine Buddha Mantra
summary: When illness comes, many Taiwanese think of him -- the Medicine Master of Lapis Lazuli Light Tathagata, teacher of the Eastern Pure Lapis Lazuli World, who made twelve great vows for the one purpose of lifting the suffering of the sick. To recite the Medicine Buddha Mantra is to pray for health, for illness eased, for calamity averted and life extended.
content:
The Medicine Buddha Mantra is the root mantra of the Medicine Master of Lapis Lazuli Light Tathagata (Medicine Buddha), drawn from the Sutra on the Merits and Original Vows of the Medicine Master of Lapis Lazuli Light Tathagata. The Medicine Buddha presides over the Eastern Pure Lapis Lazuli World and made twelve great vows whose heart is to relieve all sentient beings of the suffering of body and mind. In Taiwan both this devotion and the recitation of the mantra are widespread -- above all when you yourself, or someone in your family, has fallen ill.

【Full Text of the Mantra】
The complete mantra is: "Namo bhagavate bhaishajya-guru vaidurya-prabha-rajaya tathagataya arhate samyak-sambuddhaya. Tadyatha: Om bhaishajye bhaishajye bhaishajya-samudgate svaha."
The essential short form is: "Om bhaishajye bhaishajye bhaishajya-samudgate svaha."

【The Twelve Great Vows of the Medicine Buddha】
While still on the path of causal cultivation, the Medicine Buddha made twelve great vows; the ones that touch healing most directly are these:
- The Sixth Great Vow (Completeness of Faculties): that all sentient beings have healthy, complete bodies, with all six sense faculties intact, free from disability and suffering.
- The Seventh Great Vow (Peace of Body and Mind): that all impoverished and ill sentient beings receive medical treatment and come to physical and mental well-being.
- The Eleventh Great Vow (Satisfaction and Happiness): that all sentient beings tormented by hunger and thirst be satiated.
These great vows are what hold up the healing heart of Medicine Buddha devotion.

【Methods and Timing of Recitation】
- Daily health maintenance: recite the Medicine Buddha Mantra 49 or 108 times a day, dedicating the merit to your own and your family's health.
- During illness: recite for yourself or a sick loved one, the more the better; before the Medicine Buddha statue you may also light "Medicine Buddha Lamps" (typically seven or forty-nine) as you recite and pray.
- Special practice: recitation is said to carry special force on the Medicine Buddha's birthday (the 30th day of the ninth lunar month), and some practice centers hold "Medicine Buddha Dharma Assemblies" to recite the Medicine Buddha Sutra and mantra together.
- Medicine Buddha blessed water: bless clean water by reciting the Medicine Buddha Mantra 49 times, then drink it or apply it to the affected area -- a folk healing method widely practiced in Taiwan.

【Medicine Buddha Lamps and Longevity Assemblies】
At major Buddhist temples across Taiwan, "lighting Medicine Buddha Lamps" is a very popular way to pray. A worshipper lights a lamp for themselves or a family member (usually for an entire year), asking the Medicine Buddha's protection to avert calamity, extend life, and keep the body well. The ever-burning flame symbolizes the Medicine Buddha's radiance dispelling darkness and disease. Each year temples also hold "Medicine Buddha Longevity Dharma Assemblies," reciting the Medicine Buddha Sutra and mantra together to bless all who come.

【Current State of Devotion in Taiwan】
Medicine Buddha devotion has long thrived in Taiwan; notable centers include Medicine Buddha Temple in Taipei, Ciming Temple in Taichung, and Guangde Temple in Kaohsiung. During the COVID-19 pandemic, many Buddhist organizations called on the faithful to recite the Medicine Buddha Mantra together and dedicate the merit toward a swift end of the outbreak -- proof that this ancient devotion still holds its force in modern society.

title: The Rebirth Mantra (Wangsheng Zhou)
summary: When someone close dies, the first thing many Taiwanese do is recite this mantra for them -- the Rebirth Mantra, in full the "Dharani for Pulling Out the Roots of All Karmic Obstacles and Gaining Rebirth in the Pure Land," which clears away the departed's karmic obstacles and guides them toward the Western Pure Land.
content:
The Rebirth Mantra, formally titled "The Dharani for Pulling Out the Roots of All Karmic Obstacles and Gaining Rebirth in the Pure Land," is one of the most important mantras in Taiwanese Buddhist funerary customs and memorial dharma assemblies. Whenever a loved one passes away, reciting a passage of the Rebirth Mantra is the most common way Taiwanese people give voice to remembrance and blessing.

【Full Text of the Mantra】
"Namo amitabhaya, tathagataya, tadyatha, amritabhave, amrita, siddham bhave, amrita, vikrante, amrita, vikranta, gamini, gagana, kirti-kare, svaha."

【Meaning of the Mantra】
The full title alone -- "Pulling Out the Roots of All Karmic Obstacles and Gaining Rebirth in the Pure Land" -- says plainly what it does: to uproot the accumulated karmic obstacles the deceased has gathered over many lives, so that they may be reborn in Amitabha Buddha's Western Pure Land. The word "amrita" (meaning "nectar" or "deathless") recurs throughout the mantra, and is itself another transliteration of Amitabha Buddha's name -- the Buddha's infinite radiance and dharma nectar washing the deceased clean of their karmic transgressions.

【When and How to Recite】
- Deathbed chanting: as a loved one is dying, family members and dharma friends gather to chant "Namo Amitabha Buddha" with the Rebirth Mantra woven through, guiding the dying to let go of attachment and turn toward the Pure Land.
- During the funeral period: from the moment of death, continuous chanting of the Buddha's name and the Rebirth Mantra continues for at least eight hours (Buddhism holds that in this span the deceased's consciousness has not yet fully departed and can still hear the chanting). It is recited widely at memorial services and dharma assemblies as well.
- Memorial dharma assemblies: through the 49 days after death, a "seven-day" assembly is held every seventh day for salvation ceremonies, with the Rebirth Mantra at the center.
- Daily dedication: in ordinary daily practice, 21 recitations of the Rebirth Mantra are dedicated to all karmic creditors from past lives and to deceased relatives -- a common daily practice for Taiwanese Buddhists.
- Tomb-sweeping during Qingming Festival: recited at gravesites or columbaria, praying that ancestors may rest peacefully in the Pure Land.

【Companion Scriptures】
The Rebirth Mantra is usually recited together with the Amitabha Sutra. The complete sequence runs: first recite the Amitabha Sutra once, then chant "Namo Amitabha Buddha" a set number of times, then recite the Rebirth Mantra a set number of times, closing with a verse of dedication. This set is the fundamental daily practice of the Pure Land school in Taiwan.

【Influence on Taiwanese Society】
The Rebirth Mantra is woven deep into Taiwan's culture of life and death. Even people who rarely set foot in a Buddhist temple will generally recite it a few times when a loved one dies. Many funeral service providers play recordings of the Rebirth Mantra or set out electronic chanting devices at memorial services, filling the hall with solemn sutra sound. In recent years, as the practice of preparing advance directives has grown, many people note in their wills that they wish to be sent off at death with chanting of the Buddha's name and the Rebirth Mantra -- one measure of just how deeply this devotion is rooted in Taiwanese society.

title: The Shurangama Mantra (Lengyan Zhou)
summary: Over two thousand characters, 427 lines -- the longest mantra in Buddhism, the Shurangama Mantra, revered as the "King of Mantras." It is said that for as long as it circulates in the world, the True Dharma abides in the world, and in Chan temples the monastics recite it every dawn.
content:
The Shurangama Mantra comes from the Shurangama Sutra (The Sutra of the Heroic March). At more than 2,000 characters in length (five sections and 427 lines), it is the longest mantra in Buddhism and is revered as the "King of Mantras." In the Chinese Buddhist tradition it is more than that: it is a symbol of the True Dharma's continued presence in the world, for as the sutra says, as long as the Shurangama Mantra remains in circulation, the Buddha's teachings endure.

【Status of the Mantra】
The Shurangama Sutra records that when the Buddha proclaimed this mantra, the Buddhas of all ten directions sent forth light at once, and countless Vajra Treasury King Bodhisattvas and heavenly dharma protectors gathered to uphold it. The scripture presses the point: "If this mantra is destroyed, then all demon kings, ghosts, spirits, and non-Buddhist practitioners will have free rein." For that reason, reciting the Shurangama Mantra is taken as the most powerful weapon for protecting the True Dharma and subduing demonic forces. In the monasteries of Chinese Buddhism -- the Chan (Zen) temples -- it is the centerpiece of the morning service, and every monastic is required to recite it daily.

【Five-Section Structure】
The Shurangama Mantra falls into five sections (wu hui), each with its own function:
- First section: summons all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and dharma protectors, and establishes the altar boundary.
- Second section: subdues celestial demons and non-Buddhist forces, compelling them to take refuge in the True Dharma.
- Third section: breaks every malevolent spell and sorcery.
- Fourth section: subdues all ghosts, spirits, and supernatural entities.
- Fifth section: gathers up all the blessings, ensuring ultimate benefit for the reciter.
The "Shurangama Mantra Heart" -- a condensed core section drawn from the full mantra -- is sometimes recited by those who cannot manage the entire mantra.

【Memorization and Practice】
For all its extraordinary length, committing the Shurangama Mantra to memory is a formidable challenge. In Taiwan's Buddhist academies and monastic training, memorizing it is a basic requirement, and many lay practitioners also vow to do the same -- a process that usually takes three to six months of intensive practice. Common methods of cultivation:
- Monastic morning service: one complete recitation each dawn, about twenty to thirty minutes.
- Intensive practice: 108 recitations make up one complete major practice cycle.
- Boundary protection: recited after setting up a home altar to create a protective boundary and keep the household's spiritual purity.

【Practice in Taiwan】
All the major Buddhist monasteries in Taiwan (such as Chung Tai Chan Monastery, Dharma Drum Mountain, and Fo Guang Shan) include the Shurangama Mantra among the required texts of the morning liturgy. Many temples also hold "Shurangama Assemblies," where devotees recite the entire Shurangama Sutra and mantra together. In folk practice it is regarded as the most powerful of protective mantras; some devotees carry it on their person (as a miniature scroll or protective amulet), trusting it to ward off evil, deflect harm, and keep them safe.

title: The Scripture of Constant Clarity and Stillness (Qingjing Jing)
summary: Just about four hundred characters, yet it is the basic text of morning and evening service in Taiwan's Taoist temples -- the Qingjing Jing, in full "The Scripture of Constant Clarity and Stillness as Spoken by the Supreme Lord Lao." It teaches the way of clarity, stillness, and effortless action (wu wei), and many recite it at dawn and dusk to settle the mind.
content:
The Scripture of Constant Clarity and Stillness (full title: "The Scripture of Constant Clarity and Stillness as Spoken by the Supreme Lord Lao"), commonly known as the Qingjing Jing, is generally shortened to its brief name. In little more than 400 characters it distills the core of Taoist cultivation -- "clarity, stillness, and non-action" (qingjing wuwei). In the Taoist temples of Taiwan it is the most basic of the texts recited at morning and evening liturgy.

【Core Philosophy】
The Qingjing Jing opens: "The Great Tao has no form, yet it gives birth to heaven and earth; the Great Tao has no feeling, yet it moves the sun and moon; the Great Tao has no name, yet it nourishes all things." It names three marks of the Tao -- formless, without feeling, and nameless -- and yet it gives birth to heaven and earth, turns the sun and moon, and nurtures all living things. One who cultivates the Tao should take after that clear and still nature: "Looking inward at one's heart, there is no heart; looking outward at one's form, there is no form; looking far at things, there are no things. Having realized these three, one perceives only emptiness." Look inward, and you see that heart, form, and phenomena are all, at root, empty and still, and the state of clarity and stillness has arrived.

The scripture then puts its finger on the trouble: "The reason sentient beings cannot attain the True Tao is that they possess deluded minds." The root of every affliction is this deluded mind -- its false discrimination and attachment. Only when one can "banish desire, and the mind naturally becomes still; clarify the mind, and the spirit naturally becomes clear" does it follow that "naturally the six desires do not arise and the three poisons are extinguished," reaching at last "constant response, constant stillness, constant clarity and stillness."

【Methods of Recitation】
- Daily practice: recite once each morning and once each evening, about five to ten minutes; before you begin, burn incense and bow three times to the Three Pure Ones.
- Tempo and intonation: keep it slow and solemn. Taoist scripture recitation has its own distinctive rhythm and tonal pattern ("dao qiang," or Taoist chant), and each ritual altar carries its own characteristic style.
- Seated meditation: after reciting, sit quietly for a period to taste the state those two words -- clarity, stillness -- point to.
- Scripture copying: as Buddhists copy the Heart Sutra, Taoist devotees copy the Qingjing Jing as a form of cultivation of their own.

【Comparison with the Buddhist Heart Sutra】
What is striking is how close the Taoist Qingjing Jing and the Buddhist Heart Sutra sit -- in length, in function, and in their core philosophy:
- Length: the Qingjing Jing runs about 400 characters, the Heart Sutra about 260 -- both short, essential core scriptures.
- Function: both are daily recitation texts meant to settle the mind.
- Core concepts: the Qingjing Jing speaks of "emptiness" and "clarity and stillness," the Heart Sutra of "emptiness" and "freedom from hindrance" -- different roads to the same destination.
That likeness mirrors the deep tradition of Buddhist-Taoist synthesis in Chinese religious culture.

【Practice in Taiwan】
Taoist temples across Taiwan (such as Zhinan Temple in Taipei, the Altar of Heaven in Tainan, and Lecheng Temple in Taichung) recite the Qingjing Jing during morning and evening services. Many Taoist devotees make it their daily practice: a recitation at dawn to settle the mind, another at nightfall to cleanse the day's afflictions. In Taiwanese folk religion it is also treated as a kind of protective scripture -- a small booklet carried on the body, or the text engraved on a protective amulet, believed to ward off evil and keep one safe.

title: Treatise on Response and Retribution (Taishang Ganying Pian)
summary: "Calamity and fortune have no gate; they are summoned by people themselves. The retribution of good and evil follows like a shadow." With those opening lines, the Treatise on Response and Retribution -- hailed as "the world's foremost book of virtue" -- lays out cause and effect in some 1,700 characters and has shaped, to its depths, the Taiwanese folk sense of reward and retribution.
content:
The Treatise on Response and Retribution (Taishang Ganying Pian) is the most famous moral tract in Taoism, hailed as "the world's foremost book of virtue." In roughly 1,700 characters it proclaims the principles of karmic cause and effect in the name of the Supreme Lord Lao (Taishang Laojun). Its opening is that very declaration -- "Calamity and fortune have no gate; they are summoned by people themselves. The retribution of good and evil follows like a shadow" -- two short sentences that have shaped, to their depths, the concept of moral causation in Taiwanese folk religion.

【Core Philosophy】
The Treatise's central claim is plain: a person's fortune and misfortune are not randomly bestowed by heaven but drawn to them by their own good and evil actions. Between heaven and earth there exist "officers who record transgressions," documenting every person's deeds -- good deeds increase blessings and extend life, while evil deeds diminish blessings and shorten life. The text lists out, one by one, kinds of virtuous conduct (such as loyalty, filial piety, friendship, compassion toward orphans and widows, and kindness without expectation of return) and kinds of evil (such as deceit in a dark room, exploiting subordinates for personal credit, and flattering superiors while deceiving those below) -- a practical ruler to measure daily conduct against.

【The Merit and Demerit Ledger】
Under the Treatise's influence, Taiwanese folk tradition grew its own practice of the "merit and demerit ledger" (gongguo ge) -- each night before sleep you take out a ledger and set down the day's good deeds (merits) and bad deeds (demerits), then look back over the balance from time to time. This practice of self-reflection was extremely popular during the Qing Dynasty, and many phoenix halls (temples that practice spirit-writing divination) continue to promote the merit and demerit ledger today.

【Influence in Taiwan】
The Treatise on Response and Retribution runs so deep in Taiwanese folk religion as to be nearly everywhere:
- Karmic retribution: the idea that "good is rewarded with good, evil with evil" is a cornerstone of Taiwanese folk belief.
- City God and officers of record: Taiwan's City God temples are known for their plaques reading "Good and evil will ultimately meet their just reward," a direct echo of the Treatise.
- Moral tract tradition: temples throughout Taiwan freely distribute moral tracts, and the Treatise is among the most common.
- Phoenix hall culture: many phoenix halls use the Treatise as their core text for educating and edifying devotees.

【Methods of Reading and Practice】
- Daily practice: read the Treatise once a day, reflecting on your own conduct against it.
- Vowing to distribute: printing copies of the Treatise for free distribution is one of the most common ways of "accumulating merit" in Taiwanese folk culture.
- Combined practice: keep a merit and demerit ledger of your daily deeds, examining yourself against the Treatise.

Though the Treatise on Response and Retribution is a Taoist text, its principles of karmic cause and effect and its spirit of moral exhortation long ago crossed the lines of religion to become a vital part of the moral fabric of Taiwanese society.
